Boombox
BOOM-boks
noun (Gen X slang)
From boom (imitative of a deep, resonant sound) + box; American slang of the late 1970s and early 1980s for the large portable radio-cassette players, often with twin decks and big speakers, made by Japanese firms such as JVC, Sharp, and Panasonic. The boombox belongs first of all to the Black and Latino youth of New York, whose block parties, breakdancing circles, and early hip-hop made it an instrument of the culture; LL Cool J saluted it in "I Can’t Live Without My Radio" (1985). Two films of 1989 fixed it in memory: Radio Raheem’s radio in Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing, and John Cusack holding a boombox overhead playing Peter Gabriel’s "In Your Eyes" in Say Anything….

Biblical Definition

The boombox was the portable stereo of the 1980s: big enough to carry on the shoulder, loud enough to fill a park, with a cassette deck for the latest tape and a radio for the latest station. Hip-hop grew up around it; breakdancers spun to it on flattened cardboard; teenagers carried it to the beach and the basketball court. It was music meant to be shared, out loud, with everyone in earshot. The Christian observation has two sides. First, Scripture is not shy of loud music. "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise" (Psa 98:4). "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3). God built ears to enjoy sound that fills a space. Second, loud music carried among neighbors raises the question of love. Proverbs has a wry word for the man who blesses his friend "with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him" (Pro 27:14). Paul’s rule is simple: "Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification" (Rom 15:2). And noise without love is only noise: "sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" (1Co 13:1). A father can show his children the old boombox in the attic, play something joyful on it loud, and teach them both lessons: God loves a joyful noise, and love turns the volume down when the neighbor’s baby is asleep.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X name (late 1970s–80s, New York hip-hop and beyond) for the big portable radio-cassette player; Scripture loves a joyful loud noise (Psa 98:4) and asks that it please the neighbor (Rom 15:2).

BOOMBOX, n. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–1980s, US urban speech) A large portable stereo radio with cassette player and built-in speakers, carried by hand or on the shoulder. "He brought the boombox to the park and everybody started dancing."

Also boom box, jambox; often twin-deck for dubbing tapes; companion of breakdancing, block parties, and early hip-hop.

Film icons: Radio Raheem in Do the Right Thing (1989); the Say Anything… serenade (1989).

Webster 1828: BOOM, v.i. 1. In marine language, to rush with violence, as a ship under a press of sail. 2. To swell; to roll and roar, as waves. The hoarse waves booming to the ocean shore. 3. To cry as the bittern. The Dutch use bom for the sound of an empty barrel, and bommen is to drum.

Decode for parents: the boombox made music a public, shared thing; keep the joy and add the neighbor.

Key Scripture

Psa 98:4 — "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise."

Psa 33:3 — "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise."

Pro 27:14 — "He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him."

Rom 15:2 — "Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification."

1Co 13:1 — "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."

Modern Corruption

The boombox made music loud, public, and joyful, and sometimes inconsiderate; Scripture blesses the joyful loud noise and asks that it be made in love for the neighbor.

expand to see more

Joy that is shared. The boombox has an honorable history: it carried music into streets and parks where people gathered, and it helped birth a whole culture of dance and rhyme in New York neighborhoods. That is closer to the Psalter than the private headphone ever was. The Psalms are loud and public: make a loud noise, and rejoice (Psa 98:4); play skilfully with a loud noise (Psa 33:3). Music meant to be heard together is a gift.

Noise without love. But the same box at two in the morning under an open window is a different thing. Proverbs laughs at the man whose loud blessing at dawn is counted a curse (Pro 27:14). Volume is not neutral when someone else has to live in it. Paul’s rule settles it: please your neighbour for his good (Rom 15:2). Without charity even angelic music becomes sounding brass (1Co 13:1). A family that loves music can keep both rules at once: sing loud at the right hour, and turn the knob down the moment a neighbor is burdened by it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Imitative boom + box → late-1970s New York street and hip-hop culture → 1980s portable stereo → Do the Right Thing and Say Anything… (1989); Scripture: make a joyful noise (Psa 98:4), please thy neighbour (Rom 15:2).

"Please your neighbour for his good (Rom 15:2) — and turn it down at midnight."
